I have heard a physician pointing out the analogy between the Four Truths and his own British medical code, simply from hearing them stated as Buddhist religious doctrine, without allusion being made to his own profession. Talking of physicians tempts me to quote from the letter of a notable British Buddhist as bearing on this point: “The operation and hospital-experience was indeed a very formidable affair—so terribly impressive in its insistence on the *Dukkha*-Truths, that I marvel... after that experience, that the realization of the truth of them is not more common, at least among those who have to do with hospitals. Perhaps indeed this most impressive object-lesson is responsible for the large proportion of medical men among those Occidentals who are... deeply interested in Buddhism.”

Moreover, to quote the late Commentary on the *Yogasutras* as an authority for the statement that Indian medical procedure suggested a fundamental doctrine of Buddhism is much like saying that J. S. ### ARAB INFLUENCE IN SPAIN.

"There is a striking degree of similarity between many of the airs which I have heard in Egypt and some of the popular melodies of Spain." (Lane, "Modern Egyptians.") "Not only do we meet with certain terms and expressions in the popular songs of Spain," says Engel in his "Study of National Music," "which forcibly remind us of Arabic music, but also several Spanish instruments are of Arabic origin." 

Strange to say, Engel failed to mention the dances of Spain, which bear a wholesale imprint from the Arab: the *Sarabande*, *Villarro*, *Pabana*, *Chaconne*, *Villota*, *Maya*, *Giga*, *Gallarda*, etc. Engel points out that whilst there is little trace of Arab music in the Catholic church music in Spain, there is considerable influence to be seen in the music of the Jewish synagogue. This latter is also testified by De Sola in his "Ancient Melodies of the Spanish and Portuguese Jews" (1857).

# III THE BULL-DIONYSUS

The representation of wood-spirits in goat-form appears to be both widespread and, to the primitive mind, natural. Therefore, when we find that Dionysus—a tree-god—is sometimes represented in goat form, we can hardly avoid the conclusion that this representation is simply part of his character as a tree-god, rather than a fusion of two independent cults—one a tree-god cult and the other a goat-god cult. If such a fusion occurred for Dionysus, it must also have occurred for the Pans and Satyrs of Greece, the Fauns of Italy, and the *Ljeschie* of Russia. That such a fusion of disconnected cults occurred once is possible; that it occurred twice independently is improbable; and that it occurred three times is practically incredible.

Dionysus was also represented, as we have seen, in the form of a bull. We are led to expect that his bull form is just another expression of his character as a vegetation deity, especially since the bull is a common embodiment of the corn-spirit in Northern Europe, and his association with Demeter and Proserpine at Eleusis shows he had strong agricultural affinities. The only other possible explanation is that the bull-conception was originally distinct and was merged due to something like the union of two tribes (a view suggested by Mr. Andrew Lang).

*Festivals.* There is no act of uniformity and no ecclesiastical calendar regulating the festivals or forms of worship of village deities, and no universal custom as to the appointment of ministrants. In some villages, where there is a permanent shrine, offerings of rice, fruit, and flowers, with incense and camphor, are made every day by the villagers who have made vows to the goddess, through the pūjārī . Often offerings are made once or twice a week, on fixed days, consisting chiefly of grain, fruit, and flowers, and occasionally of goats, sheep, and fowls. In many places there is a fixed annual festival, which sometimes takes place after harvest when the people are at leisure and have plenty of food; but there is no regular rule as to the time, and the custom varies widely in different districts. In most places, however, there is no regular annual festival, but sacrifices are offered whenever an epidemic or any other calamity occurs which may make it expedient to propitiate the goddess. In some villages, old men complained to me that whereas formerly sacrifices were offered yearly, now, owing to the decay of religion, they are only offered once in four or five years. So, again, there is no uniformity as to the duration of a festival. Generally it lasts about a week, but in the Tamil country it is sometimes a very elaborate affair, lasting for a fortnight, three weeks, or even a whole month; so too in some parts of the Canarese country, the Māri festival, which is held in February, lasts for about four weeks. But a long festival is an expensive luxury that only a large town or a well-to-do village is able to afford. Speaking generally, the object of the festival is simply to propitiate the goddess.

Every village in South India is believed by the people to be surrounded by evil spirits, who are always on the watch to inflict diseases and misfortunes of all kinds on the unhappy villagers. They lurk everywhere—on the tops of palmyra trees, in caves and rocks, in ravines and chasms. They fly about in the air like birds of prey, ready to pounce down upon any unprotected victim, and the Indian villagers pass through life in constant dread of these invisible enemies. So the poor people turn for protection to the guardian deities of their village, whose function it is to ward off these evil spirits and protect the village from epidemics of cholera, smallpox, or fever, as well as from cattle disease, crop failure, childlessness, fires, and all the manifold ills that flesh is heir to in an Indian village.

The sole object, then, of the worship of these village deities is to propitiate them and to avert their wrath. There is no idea of praise or thanksgiving, no expression of gratitude or love, and no desire for any spiritual or moral blessings. The one object is to get rid of cholera, smallpox, cattle disease, or drought, or to avert some of the minor evils of life. The worship, therefore, in most of the villages, only takes place occasionally. SINCE IT IS THE CUSTOM of our Academy that we attempt to teach everything that the human mind can attain, it behooves us teachers to have learned everything, a state we have not yet reached. For I do not see that any of us could have promised that to himself, nor, as I feel, has anyone done so. Or if he has promised it, he did so more out of zeal and desire than out of knowledge of a difficult and arduous matter. If someone were to read all the books of Plato, or even those of Aristotle, or Plutarch as well: how many are there who do not think they have heard, inquired into, and known everything? Yet how many and how great are the things they lacked? I believe indeed, and I believe truly: if one were to gather and arrange in order the doctrines of all philosophers, whether they be Epicureans, or Academics of both the old and new Academy, or Stoics—of all these, I say, and of the rest of the wise men of all Greece—yet one would see that they wished for everything rather than were able to, and that they had divided rather than explained whatever philosophy professes. And even if there were nothing else: they could certainly say nothing about God, nothing about the creation of the world, nothing about the nature of man, and nothing about the return of men into life. "Difficult are the things that are beautiful," said Solon. Plato asserted that goodness accompanies difficulty. But Aristotle, Prince and Leader of philosophers, testified that virtue and art reside in difficult things. Indeed, it is true; thus, while the art and science of Medicine is most beautiful, it exists as a difficult thing, which, however, goodness and utility accompany: such as health itself, peace of mind, and among the wise, the highest honor. Moved and stirred by these things, the most august Emperors of the Romans, the most invincible Kings, and the highest Pontiffs of our ages, delighted greatly in this study. For that Augustus Caesar gladly used a medical composition invented by himself, which later many Physicians translated into their own books. Nero, that tyrant and indeed unpraised, yet truly most learned, is said to have placed a part of his study in this genre. Tiberius Caesar, according to Galen, composed troches for shingles. ## CHAPTER VI.

### *History of Typhon.*

Diodorus makes Typhon born of the Titans. Plutarch says he is the brother of Osiris and Isis: some others advance that he was born from the Earth, when Juno irritated struck it with her foot; that the fear he had of Jupiter made him flee to Egypt, where, unable to endure the heat of the climate, he threw himself into a lake where he perished. Hesiod gives us a most atrocious depiction of him , which Apollodorus seems to have copied. The Earth, they say, outraged with fury that Jupiter had struck the Titans with his thunderbolts, joined with Tartarus, and making one last effort, she gave birth to Typhon. This dreadful monster had a greatness and a strength superior to all the others combined. His height was so enormous that he far surpassed the highest mountains, and his head penetrated to the stars. His extended arms reached from the orient to the occident, and from his hands came one hundred furious dragons,

Countless vipers issued from his legs and thighs, and folding back in various convolutions, stretched the entire length of his body, with hisses so horrible they astonished the most intrepid. His mouth exhaled nothing but flames; his eyes were burning coals, and his voice was more terrible than thunder; at times he bellowed like a bull, at times he roared like a lion, and sometimes he barked like a dog. CaG The whole upper part of his body was bristling with feathers, and the lower part was covered in scales. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods, who dared to throw rocks and mountains against Heaven while letting out frightful howls. The Gods were so terrified by this that, not believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and sheltered themselves from the pursuits of this monster by hiding under the forms of various animals.

Attempts have been made to explain what ancient authors said about Typhon from moral, historical, and physical perspectives. The applications made have sometimes been quite successful, but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within a single system. His marriage with Echidna made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Sphinx, the Eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.
